about.heading: About
about.headline: Most people do one part of this. Caio does the span.
about.bio:
Caio Ogata is a Creative Designer. A former art director with a background in user interfaces and a self-taught path into development. He is happiest building sites that tell a story the way a photograph does. Through what you see and feel, rather than by explaining themselves.

Cinema and photography came first, years before either was work. Framing, composition, colour, the way a shot moves. Technology ran alongside them, in video games and computers, and it is the more logical half of how he thinks. Advertising was where the looking became work.

Nothing on the screen is there by accident. Type, grid, motion and interaction all do a job, and they get decided together. He designs the experience and writes the code that makes it behave.

The craft comes from advertising. Several years in agencies as an art director, then a specialisation at Miami Ad School in São Paulo. The discipline there is making an idea land in a single look.

Huia is where the two halves met. He joined the creative technology studio in 2013 and stayed eight years, six of them as partner. The brief was rarely a layout. It was a question: can this be built? The answers ran on WebGL, facial recognition and machine learning, years before any of that was ordinary. He led creative direction for Petrobras, O Boticário, Tramontina, Sicredi and Mondelez brands. He also picked up the habit he still works by, which is to build a rough one early and look at it.

Azion Technologies hired him to build a design operation from nothing, inside a company of engineers. He grew it to fourteen people across five disciplines. Four years, three roles: design, then brand, then the tools engineers use. Sitting that close to engineering taught him the other half of the job. How software actually ships, what a component costs, why an engineer says no.

Most people who do this work do one part of it. Caio does the span. The idea, the way it looks, and the thing that actually runs. For a client that means one person from start to finish.

items.title: Azion Website & Brand Expansion
items.description: A brand stretch, not a rebuild. The site needed more range — richer layouts, stronger colour, a way to show what the product actually does — without throwing away the front-end already running in production.
items.technologies: Astro, Vue.js, Webkit Component Library, Design Tokens, Sora Typography, Monospace, Brand Adaptation, Illustration System
items.impact: New illustration patterns that explain features visually. Richer page blocks across every page. The existing architecture survived intact.

sections.body: A brand adaptation that evolved Azion's digital presence while preserving the technology already in production.

sections.challenge: Azion needed to expand its visual identity without breaking the existing front-end architecture built on Astro and Vue.
sections.solution: We evolved the existing system by introducing new color tones, richer block variants, and an illustration pattern that visually represents product features.

sections.body: Below, the pieces that hold the site together — the navigation, the documentation, the component library, and the brand concept behind them.

items.title: Azion Console Kit
items.description: The screen engineers use to deploy and watch their applications, rebuilt from scratch. Vue 3, a shared component library, and an architecture that separates how a screen looks from what it does.
items.technologies: Vue 3, Vite, PrimeVue, TypeScript, Design Tokens, Component Architecture, Headless UI Pattern, Open Source
items.impact: Open source: 6,000+ commits, 34+ contributors, 93+ releases. In production at Itaú, Magazine Luiza and Netshoes. New screens went from days to hours. Caio led it; the team he built wrote it.

sections.body: The complete front-end rebuild of Azion's management console — the interface engineers use daily to deploy, secure, and observe applications at the edge.

sections.challenge: The legacy console was a monolithic application that slowed feature delivery and created inconsistent experiences across product surfaces.
sections.solution: Built a headless architecture on Vue 3 that decouples UI from business logic, with block componentization that reduced new screen implementation time to approximately one day.

philosophy.heading: Philosophy
philosophy.title: Fall, learn, evolve
philosophy.body:
Good design comes from the same place as good athleticism: a willingness to fail, learn, and go again.

Caio learned it on a judo mat. As he wrote in 2018: "In Judo, the first lessons are all focused on teaching how to fall. From the beginning, it's understood that you will fall, lose, err. So suffer less, lose the fear, preserve your body and, most importantly, prepare your mind for the obstacles ahead."

Skateboarding taught him the same thing. Skaters are the most persistent people he has met. They fall hundreds of times learning one trick, and do it without fear, because falling is the process rather than a failure of it.

It translates directly. The best work comes from teams that are not afraid to test, fail and change. Ship early, get it in front of people, keep going. Nothing good arrives finished.

Running a team, he tries to build places where people can fall safely. Where iterating is the point, not a setback. Where "I don't know yet" is a fine answer, as long as curiosity and action follow it.

lifestyle.heading: Life Outside Design
lifestyle.body:
I'm a triathlete, training 10-14 hours per week across running, cycling, and swimming. The discipline of athletic training—waking at 5 AM for a two-hour run, then putting in a full workday—teaches you to manage energy, focus on what matters, and push through discomfort.

Video games have been a lifelong passion and a major influence on my design work. I've always looked at games as inspiration—particularly for visual references and interaction design. The attention to detail in game UI/UX, the storytelling through visuals, and the immersive experiences have shaped how I approach digital product design.

Before design consumed my life, music did. I played bass in INFUSE, a melodic punk rock band. I'm a cinephile who watches every Oscar nominee each year (favorite directors: Tarantino, Wes Anderson, Almodovar, Scorsese, Nolan, Villeneuve).

I'm also a three-time Brazilian vice-champion in youth baseball categories, played volleyball at the state championship level at 17, and surfed for years. I'm an INTP—analytical, curious, always questioning. I work to balance my natural tendency to question everything with the need to ship and execute.
